entries.title: The first real write to App Store Connect, and the bug only a live call could find
entries.body: The screenshot upload had been “implemented, never exercised” since July. Yesterday it made its first call: one test screenshot onto an unreleased version of Snagg, an app I own — 200 in 2.5 s, checksum matched, asset COMPLETE. The set-create branch nobody had reached ran next, also 200. Then the experiment create from the same month came back 404: the v2 endpoint had been built on a v1 path, and the read side used that path and worked, so every test believed the write side too. Fixed in an hour; the second attempt created a stopped experiment. With the writes proven, the agent can now execute an approved run itself — draft version, copy, each approved locale, every step recorded — off by default, and never on an approval older than the switch. Test assets deleted afterwards. Approving is still the last thing a person does; nothing submits.

entries.title: The MCP server shipped in July. The roadmap still said “deferred.”
entries.body: Taking stock before the growth push: 31 plugin skills, 12 live MCP tools, one GitHub star — a distribution gap, not a product gap. And the roadmap’s own second channel, the hosted MCP server, turned out to have been answering in production since July while the PRD called it deferred — and the whole endpoint sat behind login, so a stranger couldn’t even list the tools. The overnight loop opened four PRs: a public tier so `claude mcp add shipaso` works with no key and no account (a measured preview of any app, plus the aggregate proof — the two things already public on the site; every other tool answers with where a free key comes from), the docs saying what is true, and a registry manifest prepared but not published. Unchanged: no MCP tool can write to a store. Approving is still a human’s click.

entries.title: Rejected again — and the bug was in the instructions, not the app
entries.body: 0.1.1 came back on Guideline 2.1(a): “the Connect button was not responsive after sign in,” on an iPad. We went looking for a broken button and found something worse. Sign-in is passwordless, so our review notes told the reviewer to tap “Send magic link” and open the email — an email sent to a mailbox only we can read. The notes even explained why no sign-in token was included: our magic tokens expire in 15 minutes. So the reviewer had no way in, and reported the login screen as broken. They were right. Worse: after the previous rejection we had already built the fix — a 90-day review token and a “Have a sign-in token?” field, put there for exactly this. The code shipped. Nobody put the token in the notes. Today we minted one, verified it against production, and signed in on an iPad simulator to watch it work; the Connect screen we suspected turned out to be fine. Two review rounds spent on a documentation gap in front of a working feature.

entries.title: The agent's brain is now Claude
entries.body: ShipASO's reasoning and copywriting now run on Claude (Opus 5) when configured — keyword classification and, new today, genuinely authored subtitle proposals. The trust model is unchanged: the model writes, deterministic guardrails validate (hard 30-char limit, no brand words, no price claims, must carry a target keyword), and any miss falls back to the deterministic composer. An AI agent with an AI brain, still ending every run at a human's approval.

entries.title: The posting edge: proof cards become pixels, wins become posts
entries.body: The last two slices of the growth loop shipped: the proof card rasterizes to PNG where the post is sent, and a confirmed rank win now triggers the post automatically — once, with retry if X is down. A win that is really a hold or a slip posts nothing. The agent only ever brags with receipts.

entries.title: The app learned to write its own announcements
entries.body: When ShipASO moves a real organic App Store rank, it now composes the public update itself: the measured move (#40 → #12, up 28 spots), the store link, and a branded proof card rendered from the same data the dashboard shows. No genuine win, no post — the same honesty bar the product enforces everywhere.

entries.title: Subscriptions became real in-app purchases
entries.body: The compliant answer to the payments rejection: RevenueCat-powered subscriptions, bought in-app through StoreKit, with every required disclosure on the paywall. The server stays the source of truth — a verified webhook maps the purchase to a tier, and the highest active entitlement wins, so someone who already subscribed on the web can never be double-charged.

entries.title: Apple rejected 0.1.0 — on four guidelines at once
entries.body: The first App Store submission came back with four rejections: an Apple trademark in the app name, no way to buy anything (we had removed purchasing instead of building IAP), a magic link that opened a 404 instead of the app, and price text baked into screenshots. All four are fixed in 0.1.1, and the payments fix became the RevenueCat integration this whole journey runs on. Published here whichever way it goes — that is the point of this page.
